significance.justification: A verified-true result would establish that, at nearly fixed excitation energy, symmetry breaking selectively changes an internal brightness representation, that parity- and spin-forbidden transitions produce different responses, and that steering the resulting "allowedness" variable changes absorption without changing the gap. This is a form-(iii) relation between independently measurable symmetry changes, gap stability, internal signal, and oscillator strength, reinforced by a form-(ii) causal intervention; it establishes both a bright/dark counterfactual phenomenon and a mechanism that fixes expectations across families of symmetry-breaking versus symmetry-preserving edits, rather than merely finding a decodable feature. This bears directly on the regression-centric evaluation represented by QM8 in MoleculeNet (Wu et al., Chemical Science, 2018): a negative result would meaningfully show that the examined models can predict excited-state targets without implementing this established selection-rule mechanism, although it would not rule that out for foundation models generally. True and false outcomes are distinct, and the topic-substitution check lowers the generic topic alone to the median or below; the above-median score comes specifically from the claim's "parity/spin double dissociation" and matched-gap symmetry law.

reach.justification: The claim names reusable handles—the "Brightness-Beyond-Gap Index," "Symmetry-Break-vs-Preserve Causal Asymmetry," an "intensity-error failure predictor," and an "allowedness" steering direction—and explicitly proposes that they be run "before deploying a model for dark/bright-state design," making the audit and predictor ex ante rather than merely post hoc. Although the steering direction would require re-extraction per model, the substantive counterfactual relation predicts what should recur after recalibration: symmetry breaking should move brightness more than a matched symmetry-preserving edit, while parity and spin cases should dissociate. The asserted scope covers molecular/materials models used for optical-property, photochemistry, OLED-emitter, and forbidden-transition screening, giving uptake to model auditors and screening practitioners, but it does not support a general design rule across unrelated scientific domains or architectures. Under topic substitution, generic probing of scientific mechanisms would not retain this score; the extra reach comes from the quoted pre-deployment audit and transferable symmetry-response relation.
